title: Google Antigravity Pricing 2026: Plans and Limits
summary: Google Antigravity pricing ranges from free to $199.99 monthly, but quota limits are the real cost driver for automated workflows.
body_markdown:
## Cost in dollars and lost hours


$260 to $540 is what the afternoon cost in lost time, against a $19.99 subscription. That's ten to twenty-seven times the plan price, so a single outage equals ten to twenty-seven months of subscription fees.


### Antigravity Pro bill breakdown by line


Look at the invoice and there is one line: Pro at $19.99 for the month. No extra-usage charge appears in this month's math, so the bill looks cheap precisely because the real cost sits somewhere else.


Take one hour first. At the $65.38 hourly employee median, a single stalled hour costs more than three times the monthly plan, meaning even preventing one stalled hour justifies the subscription cost.


> No extra-usage charge appears in this month's math, so the bill looks cheap precisely because the real cost sits somewhere else.


The[US Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm) wage data supports three freelance rates: $85, $110 and $135 per hour for low, mid and high.


A freelancer who loses an hour is therefore out 4.3 to 6.8 times the $19.99 she paid, which costs her the equivalent of **four to seven months of subscription fees** .


Now count a four-hour afternoon, which is my assumption for a typical stall. That's about $262 at the employee median, $340 at $85, $440 at $110 and $540 at $135.


If you price the month by its subscription alone, you understate it by a factor of ten or more. A second cutoff would double those figures.


### Hidden costs and limits she hit


She couldn't see how close she was to the cap, so she couldn't schedule around it. That uncertainty was the hidden cost.


I haven't found a published figure that would let her predict the next cutoff, so I'm not offering one. What she can control is the exposure.


**If a stall costs $340 at the low freelance rate, then any cap, buffer or fallback that costs less than that per incident pays for itself the first time it prevents one.**


That's the comparison to run before choosing a plan: not $19.99 against a higher tier, but the higher tier against an afternoon.
